title: Let this cup pass
hookLine: the night before his death, Jesus prays in anguish in the garden (Matthew 26:36–39)
carry: not as I will, but as thou wilt

lines: A HYMN, THEN A GARDEN AT NIGHT.
cards: Supper is over. Matthew says they sang a hymn and went out into the mount of Olives, to a place called Gethsemane. It is night.
Jesus tells his disciples to sit and wait while he goes on to pray, and takes three of them further: Peter, and the two sons of Zebedee.
To these closest friends he says plainly how it is with him: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me." He just asks them to stay awake with him.

teach.b: First, flat on his face. Matthew says he went a little further and fell on his face. Down on the ground.
The body says it before the words do.

Second, the honest ask. Here is the prayer: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me." Some readers hear an echo of the prophets here, where a cup can stand for a hard portion someone is handed to drink.
Jesus asks, plainly, not to have to drink it. He doesn't dress the wish up as something nobler.
Third, both halves. The same breath goes on: "nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." The wish isn't taken back to make room for the trust, and the trust doesn't erase the wish.
They sit side by side in one sentence. Christians read this line in different ways. Some see in it the full humanity of Jesus, a real will that shrinks from pain.
Some see the shape of honest prayer: ask first, then let go.

Fourth, friends asleep, and a second prayer. He comes back and finds the three asleep: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" Then he goes away and prays again, and then a third time, saying the same words.
The second time, Matthew gives them as: "O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done." The first prayer asked if it be possible.
The second already sounds like a man who has heard the answer, and still calls him Father.

how: Christians read the Gethsemane story especially in Holy Week, and some keep a watch of prayer on the night of Holy Thursday, remembering the request to watch with him.

games.q: you're in the garden at night, sorrowful even unto death. you may say anything to your Father. what do you say?
o: nothing; a brave face is better
let this cup pass, and then: not as I will
games.why: he asks plainly for the cup to pass, then adds: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. the wish and the trust stay side by side.

practice: Let the hands rest open on your knees and bring to mind something hard that you wish were different.
Don't make it noble; find the plain wish underneath, I wish this weren't happening, and say it silently or in a whisper, in your own ordinary words.
If you pray, you can offer it just as it is, unpolished, the way it was said in the garden.

wordCard.voice: Gethsemane, the garden where Jesus prayed to let the cup pass, then added, not as I will, but as thou wilt. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, cup: the word in Matthew 26:39 for what Jesus asks to pass from him.
